question_text: This Indian cricketer was a prolific bowler, once the spearhead of the Indian bowling attack. He played four World Cups (taking 44 wickets) and took 551 international wickets in total. However, his performance in the second test of a 1999 test series was particularly underwhelming. In fact, in his last over in that second test, he bowled three wide balls and had a catch dropped in the same over. When asked the reason for bowling so poorly in his last over, he replied, 'Simple, I did not want to take a wicket' (paraphrase). Although it seems an excuse, it makes sense. The match ended in the next over and became special for something that is celebrated even today. What happened in the next over/last over of the match?
answer_text: Anil Kumble took all 10 wickets in the innings, finishing with bowling figures of 10/74 against Pakistan in Delhi in 1999, becoming only the second bowler in Test cricket history (after Jim Laker) to take all 10 wickets in a Test innings.

question_text: Before their actual career came along, this person auditioned for X's film Z. 'Half of New Zealand auditioned for the films, and half of New Zealand also starred in the film, except for me,' Y said in an interview. 'There was a height requirement indicated by a scale near the entrance which I obviously failed as I had to bend to go inside the door, and then they needed horseback riding and jousting. I knew how to ride a horse bareback, because, of course, half of New Zealand knows how to ride a horse bareback.' Who are we talking about?
answer_text: Jacinda Ardern, former Prime Minister of New Zealand.

answer_text: The map shows countries that allow dual citizenship: green = Recognized/Unrestricted, yellow = Restricted/Regulated, red = Prohibited except for involuntary acquisition, black = Prohibited Completely, grey = No Data.

question_text: River Monsters is a British wildlife documentary television series produced for Animal Planet by Icon Films of Bristol, United Kingdom. It is hosted by biologist Jeremy Wade, who travels around the globe in search of large and dangerous fish. It became one of the most-watched programmes in Animal Planet's history, and is also one of the most-viewed series on Discovery Channel in the American market. Jeremy Wade explored rivers and lakes to uncover the creatures behind local folklore and harrowing tales of monster fish. After the official last season in 2017, they released a one-off episode discussing host Jeremy Wade's story and his journey of making the show. Aside from not wanting to overstay their welcome, what was another reason for ending the show in 2017?
answer_text: They ran out of large river fish to talk about.

question_text: CEO Aaron Krause first started his own car washing company and filed a patent for a urethane foam he used to buff cars, while also developing another product: a ___ to wash the grease from his hands. 3M bought the formula for the buffing pads, leaving him to develop the ___ formula by himself further. Using material tailor made by a German company, he made a ___ in the shape of a ridged circle with two holes to hold his fingers, which eventually became its most popular shape. The idea to use it as a dish ___ came unexpectedly three years later, when he dipped it in a bucket of hot water and it softened, creating a scratch-free tool. Aaron accepted an offer from Shark Tank business mogul Lori Greiner, who put down US$200,000 for 20 per cent equity in the brand. When the episode aired in October 2012, the business exploded and hasn't slowed down since, making it the third largest brand of its kind in the US. It has since expanded to other products in the same product industry. What is this product?
answer_text: Scrub Daddy, the smiley-face scratch-free scrubbing sponge that changes texture with water temperature.

question_text: Connect the following / give funda: DC (Detective Comics), ATM (Automated Trailer Machine), PIN (Personal Identification Number), HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), LCD (Liquid-Crystal Display), VIN (Vehicle Identification Number).
answer_text: RAS Syndrome (Redundant Acronym Syndrome): the habit of needlessly repeating a word that is already part of the acronym, such as saying 'PIN number', 'ATM machine', 'HIV virus', 'LCD display', 'VIN number', or 'DC Comics'.

question_text: There are connections between ancient spirituality and trees influencing fortune. In the pre-Christian beliefs of the Germanic people, for example, deities send fate up into the universe through a tree. Meanwhile, the ancient Celtic peoples also believed that the act of ___ ___ called on the spirits or gods of the trees. Christians tie the practice to the symbolism of the ___ of the cross of crucifixion. Folklore researcher Steve Roud, however, suggests that the widespread, modern use derives from a form of tag called 'Tiggy ___', in which players are safe from being tagged if they are ___ ___. What term/action are we talking about?
answer_text: Knocking on wood / touchwood, i.e. touching wood for good luck.

question_text: A particular caption appears on several Japanese reality TV programs displaying any food item, to avoid getting complaints from viewers, since it is not culturally accepted in Japan to be wasting food. It is uncertain when this note was first used, but TV producer Kenji Suga stated viewers complained about the waste of food when a performance using small watermelons was broadcast in Downtown no Gaki no Tsukai ya Arahende!! on Nippon TV. The TV station then showed this note on screen the following year in response. It is also intended to teach kids about the importance of not wasting food. What does the caption say?
answer_text: The caption reads, in Japanese, that the staff ate the food item afterwards ('after this, the staff happily ate it'), so it was not wasted.

question_text: Picture clue: a 1937 rejection letter from the Editor of Nature. This paper submitted to Nature in 1937 was rejected by the Editor because Nature had such a backlog of submissions at the time that they simply couldn't look at it. The paper went on to be published in the Dutch journal Enzymologia later that year. For this work, the author won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for 'his discovery of the citric acid cycle'. Which author/research are we referring to?
answer_text: Hans Krebs and the Krebs cycle (the citric acid cycle).

question_text: Aftab Ahmed Khan, an Indian Police Service officer then serving as Additional Commissioner of Police, Mumbai, drew inspiration from the Los Angeles Police Department's Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) model, adapting it to create a force equipped for intelligence-driven operations, surveillance, and tactical interventions against armed extremists. The unit's formation responded to the need for proactive measures against groups involved in bombings, arms smuggling, and ideological radicalization, particularly in urban settings vulnerable to sudden attacks. Initially, this unit operated as a compact, elite team selected from experienced police personnel, emphasizing rapid mobilization and specialized skills over conventional policing. In response to the surge of coordinated terrorist bombings across Indian cities during the mid-2000s, this unit was spread across several states across India. Which unit of the police are we referring to?

Picture clue: a group photo of a ship's crew with one crew member circled in red. Shown in this picture within the red circle is Captain Krisnan Kanthavel. Not much is known about Captain Kanthavel, who was trained in the UK, and captained 25-men crews. In 2021, he captained a ship which on board contained a varied consignment of goods worth more than £650 million, including lemons, bamboo and tofu which is thought to have rotted away, as well as computers, laptops, mobile phones, aircraft parts, sun loungers, Ikea soft furnishings, barbecues and camping equipment which should all have been in stores months ago. Why is Captain Kanthavel famous/infamous?
answer_text: He was the captain of the Ever Given, the container ship that ran aground and blocked the Suez Canal in 2021.

question_text: Like all folk tales, this one also has unclear and debatable origins, but there are a few accepted stories. During the Pagan era, more than 600 years ago, it was common for couples to wed during the annual summer solstice, because summer was associated with fertility. It coincided with the annual migration of X and subsequent return in the spring after 9 months. The myth was further cemented in a 19th-century tale by Hans Christian Andersen, describing Xs bringing sleeping Ys to families. It has a slightly dark undertone where families with naughty kids were delivered dead Ys. What is this myth talked about?
answer_text: The myth of storks bringing/delivering babies.

question_text: After the first formal publication of a possible solution to this open problem in mathematics by the Austrian-Canadian mathematician Leo Moser in 1966, much effort has gone into establishing a lower and upper bound for the ___ constant, describing the largest possible area of a ___ fitting in an L-shaped space with arms/legs of unit width. Lower bound: an obvious lower bound is A >= pi/2, which comes from a ___ that is a half-disk of unit radius. John Hammersley derived a lower bound of pi/2 + 2/pi based on a ___ shape resembling a telephone handset. In 1992, Joseph L. Gerver of Rutgers University described a ___ formed by 18 curve sections, each taking a smooth analytic form, which further increased the lower bound for the ___ constant to approximately 2.2195. Upper bound: Hammersley found an upper bound on the ___ constant, showing that it is at most 2*sqrt(2). Yoav Kallus and Dan Romik proved a new upper bound, capping the ___ constant at 2.37. What does this mathematical model describe?
answer_text: The 'moving sofa problem' (sofa constant): the problem of finding the largest-area shape that can be moved around a right-angle corner in an L-shaped hallway of unit width.
